label: thm00
title: Theorem
body_md:
Let $T_1, \dots, T_k$ be spanning trees in a graph $G$. Then, $T_1, \dots , T_k$ are  completely independent if and only if $T_1, \dots , T_k$ are edge-disjoint and for any vertex $x \in V(G)$ and $1 \leq i \leq k$, there is at most one spanning tree $T_i$ such that $d_{T_i}(x) > 1.$
    \label{thm00}
head: environment

title: Observation
body_md: Let $G=(D\cup I, E)$ be a split graph, where $D$ is a maximal clique and $I$ is an independent set. Following \cite{lalou_completely_2026}, its corresponding hypergraph is defined as $H(G)=(D,\mathcal{E})$, such that $\mathcal{E}=\{N_G(x):x\in I\}$. Every minimal vertex separator of $G$ is the neighborhood of some vertex in $I$. Consequently, $H_S(G)$ is a subhypergraph of $H(G)$, but equality does not always hold. Therefore, the separator hypergraph representation defined here can be considered as an extension of the approach from split graphs to chordal graphs.

title: Proposition
body_md: There exists an infinite number of hypergraphs that do not satisfy Conjecture \ref{conj}.

title: Theorem
body_md: Let $G$ be a connected chordal graph. If $G$ admits $k$ CIST, then $H_C(G)$ and $H_S(G)$ both admit a panchromatic $k$-coloring.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $T_1,\dots,T_k$ be $k$ CIST of $G$. By Theorem~\ref{thm00}, every vertex of $G$ is internal in at most one tree among $T_1,\dots,T_k$. Let $\varphi$ be the $k$-coloring of $H_S(G)$ defined as follows. If a vertex $x$ is internal in $T_i$, then color $i$ is assigned to $x$. The vertices that are leaves in all the trees are assigned an arbitrary color. 

Let $S\in E(H_S(G))$ be a minimal vertex separator of $G$. By definition, there exist two vertices $u,v\in V(G)\setminus S$ that are in distinct connected components of $G-S$. For every $i \in {1,\dots,k}$, consider the unique path $P_i$ that connects $u$ and $v$ in $T_i$. Since $S$ separates $u$ and $v$ in $G$, the path $P_i$ must contain at least one vertex $x_i\in S$; therefore, $x_i$ is an internal vertex of $P_i$ and, consequently, an internal vertex of $T_i$. By the definition of $\varphi$, $x_i$ is assigned color $i$. Thus, $S$ contains at least one vertex of each color $i\in{1,\dots,k}$. It follows that every hyperedge of $H_S(G)$ contains all $k$ colors. Consequently, $\varphi$ is a panchromatic $k$-coloring of $H_S(G)$.

Also, every maximal clique of $G$ contains a minimal vertex separator which is the intersection with one of its neighboring cliques. It follows that, when extending $\varphi$ to $H_C(G)$ by assigning an arbitrary color to every vertex not belonging to $V(H_S(G))$, every hyperedge of $H_C(G)$ will contain all $k$ colors. Therefore, the extended $k$-coloring of $H_C(G)$ is panchromatic.

label: lemme0
title: Lemma
body_md:
Let $G$ be a connected chordal graph, and let $\varphi$ be a panchromatic $k$-coloring of $H_S(G)$, with color classes $D_1,\dots,D_k$. Then each $D_i$ is a connected dominating set of $G$.
\label{lemme0}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $T$ be a clique tree of $G$ such that the intersections of its endpoint cliques label its edges. These intersections are minimal vertex separators of $G$. For $i \in {1,\dots,k}$. Let $x,y\in D_i$, and let $S_x$ and $S_y$ be minimal separators containing $x$ and $y$, respectively. Over the path containing the edge labeled by $S_x$ to the one labeled by $S_y$ in $T$, every edge label is a minimal separator; therefore, it contains a vertex of color $i$. Moreover, the vertices of color $i$ that are chosen from two consecutive edge labels belong to a common maximal clique and are thus adjacent. Hence, these vertices form a path that connects $x$ to $y$, and $D_i$ is then connected. 

Let $v \in V(G)\setminus D_i$, and let $K$ be a maximal clique containing $v$. $K$ contains a minimal separator $S$. Since $\varphi$ is panchromatic, $S$ contains a vertex $x\in D_i$. And since $v,x\in K$, they are adjacent. Therefore, every vertex outside of $D_i$ has a neighbor in $D_i$. Consequently, $D_i$ is a connected dominating set of $G$.

label: thm01
title: Theorem
body_md:
Let $G$ be a connected chordal graph. If $H_S(G)$ admits a pairwise separated bipanchromatic $k$-coloring, then $G$ has $k$ CIST.
\label{thm01}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\varphi$ be a bipanchromatic $k$-coloring with color classes $D_1,\dots,D_k$. By Lemma~\ref{lemme0}, each $D_i$ is a connected dominating set of $G$. It follows that, for every $i$, the subgraph $G[D_i]$ contains a spanning tree $T'_i$ that will be used to construct a spanning tree $T_i$ in $G$. For every $j \neq i$ and every vertex $v\in D_j$, add exactly one edge of $F_{ij}^{i}$ incident with $v$, to $T_i$. Moreover, for every vertex $v\in V(G)\setminus\bigcup_{t=1}^{k}D_t$, take one neighbor $x_i \in D_i$ (this neighbor exists since $D_i$ is dominating), then add the edge $(v,x_i)$ to $T_i$. With this construction, every vertex outside $D_i$ is connected to $T_i$ by one edge. Consequently, $T_i$ is a spanning tree of $G$. Since the color classes are pairwise disjoint, the trees $T_1,\dots,T_k$ are internally disjoint.

These trees are also edge-disjoint. The edges of $T'_i$ have both extremities in $D_i$; however, every edge added to construct $T_i$ has exactly one extremity in $D_i$, which means that these edges do not belong to $T'_i$.  Since $\varphi$ is pairwise separated, for every pair $i \neq j$, the edges from $F_{ij}^{i}$ used to connect $D_j$ to $D_i$ in $T_i$ and the ones from $F_{ij}^{j}$ used to attach $D_i$ to $D_j$ in $T_j$ are edge-disjoint. Hence, $T_1,\dots,T_k$ are $k$ CIST of $G$.
head: environment

label: coro1
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{coro1}
Let G be a connected strictly chordal graph. If the separator hypergraph $H_S(G)$ admits a bipanchromatic $k$-coloring, then $G$ admits $k$ CIST.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Since the coloring is bipanchromatic, each minimal separator contains every color. Hence, for every pair of colors $i\neq j$, each vertex of $D_i$ is adjacent to a vertex of $D_j$, and vice versa. These edges in both directions can be chosen distinctly because along a clique tree, any two consecutive minimal separators are contained in a common maximal clique. Thus, the coloring is pairwise separated, and the result follows from Theorem~\ref{thm01}.
head: environment

title: Corollary
body_md: Let G be a connected strictly chordal graph and $H_S(G)$ its separator hypergraph such that $\mathcal{E}(H_S(G)) = \{ S_1,S_2, \dots, S_{\ell} \}$. If $\ell = 1$, then $G$ admits $\lfloor \frac{|S_1|}{2} \rfloor$ CIST. Otherwise, $G$ admits $S_{\min}$ CIST, with $S_{\min} = \min_{1 \leq i \leq \ell} |S_i|$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose that $\ell = 1$. Let $\{ u_1,u_2, \dots, u_{|S_1|} \}$ be the vertices of $S_1$ and let $s = \lfloor \frac{S_1}{2} \rfloor$. Let $P = \{ p_1,p_2,\dots, p_s \}$ be a set of colors. For each $i \in \{ 1,2,\dots, s \}$, assign the color $i$ to the vertices $u_{2i}$ and $u_{2i-1}$. Each color of $P$ is present twice in the hyperedge; therefore, $H_S(G)$ admits a bipanchromatic $s$-coloring. From Corollary~\ref{coro1}, $G$ admits $s$ CIST.

Now suppose that $\ell \geq 2$. For each $i \in \{ 1,2,\dots, m \}$, let $\{ v_i^1,v_i^2, \dots, v_i^{|S_i|} \}$ be the set of vertices of $S_i$. Let $P = \{ p_1,p_2,\dots, p_{|S_{\min}|} \}$ be a set of colors. For each $i$, assign the color $p_j$ to the vertex $v_i^j$. Clearly, $S_{\min}$ contains all the colors of $P$. Then, assign arbitrary colors from $P$ to the remaining uncolored vertices of $H_S(G)$. Each color in $P$ appears at least twice in each hyperedge: consequently, $H_S(G)$ admits a bipanchromatic $|S_{\min}|$-coloring. From Corollary~\ref{coro1}, $G$ admits $|S_{\min}|$ CIST.

label: thm02
title: Theorem
body_md:
Let $G$ be a connected chordal graph. If $H_S(G)$ admits a bipanchromatic $k$-coloring such that $m$ colors are total colors, then $G$ admits $\lfloor \frac{k+m}{2} \rfloor$ CIST.
\label{thm02}
